power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.065", "p = 0.060", "p = 0.060" ), Sentence = c("The resulting overall change in their relative advantage was -0.29 [-0.60, 0.01] pp (p = 0.065).", "V3 showed the largest estimated change, -1.07 pp (nominal p = 0.015, Holm-adjusted p = 0.060).", "V3 had the largest estimated change in relative model benefit (Holm-adjusted p = 0.060)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Objective.
Can a fixed V1/V6 projection of the time-embedded 3D ECG estimate the final 40 ms of V2-V5 more accurately than a fitted single lead?
Methods.
We used simultaneous recordings from the Lobachevsky University Electrocardiography Database (LUDB), with cardiologist-annotated QRS complexes in all six chest leads.
We fitted both models in 118 patients and tested them in 80 others.
Root mean squared error (RMSE) is expressed in percentage points (pp) of the target lead's 10-second amplitude range.
Results.
In 733 test beats, patient-weighted terminal RMSE fell from 12.58 to 10.64 pp (difference 1.94 pp, 95% bootstrap confidence interval 1.30 to 2.55).
Reductions were 3.23, 2.85 and 1.35 pp in V3, V4 and V5.
In V2 the difference was 0.35 pp (95% interval -0.35 to 1.05).
In 702 matched beats from 77 patients, the overall advantage was 2.22 pp at the automatic V1/V6 end and 1.92 pp at the annotated target end.
Of 1,498 beat-lead pairs with whole-QRS correlation ≥ 0.95, 28.84% still had terminal RMSE of at least 10 pp.
A fixed V1/V6 projection improved offline estimates of relative terminal amplitude in V3-V5 without fitting the target lead in the new patient.
The gain was largest in V3 and V4 and uncertain in V2.
Whether a reconstructed trace preserves a clinically recognizable notch or slur remains untested.

When a reduced-lead recording includes V1 and V6 but omits the intervening chest leads, the clinician sees the terminal QRS in two precordial leads and must infer how it might appear in the others [1].
text.formatted: When a reduced-lead recording includes V1 and V6 but omits the intervening chest leads, the clinician sees the terminal QRS in two precordial leads and must infer how it might appear in the others <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: For example, when evaluating an early repolarization pattern in V4 or V5, a reader examines the final downslope of the R wave for a notch or slur [2].
text.formatted: For example, when evaluating an early repolarization pattern in V4 or V5, a reader examines the final downslope of the R wave for a notch or slur <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: A reconstruction may follow the dominant R wave closely and still miss a smaller, later deflection.
This makes the final 40 ms a clinically relevant segment in which to test a reconstruction.
The time-embedded three-dimensional ECG plots V1 and V6 against time.
Changing the projection angle changes the contribution of each lead to the resulting trace.
Earlier work used this representation to examine precordial waveforms in STAFF III recordings [3], R-wave progression across viewing directions [4] and apparent J waves in V6 [5].
text.formatted: Earlier work used this representation to examine precordial waveforms in STAFF III recordings <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, R-wave progression across viewing directions <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> and apparent J waves in V6 <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Here the angle has a different use.

If an angle learned for V4 in one group can estimate the terminal V4 waveform in another, the same two recorded signals can provide an estimate of a lead unavailable to the reader, without individual calibration of the angle.
Nelwan et al. studied reduced lead sets, and Horáček et al. tested transformations combining limb electrodes with pairs of chest electrodes [1, 6].
text.formatted: Nelwan et al. studied reduced lead sets, and Horáček et al. tested transformations combining limb electrodes with pairs of chest electrodes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: We asked a narrower question about the two precordial inputs alone.
For which targets does the fixed projection reduce error over the final 40 ms compared with a fitted single lead?
Does the comparison change when the end of the scoring window is set by V1 and V6?
LUDB version 1.0.1 contains a 10-second, simultaneous 12-lead ECG sampled at 500 Hz for each of 200 participants.
It includes healthy volunteers and patients with cardiovascular disease.
Two LUDB cardiologists examined each lead visually and agreed on the wave onsets, peaks and ends [7, 8].

text.formatted: The distinction between the end of a complex in a single lead and its end across multiple leads has long been recognized in ECG delineation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: The choice of endpoint also changes which samples are judged.
On the same 702 beats, projection RMSE was 13.02 pp with the input-defined end and 10.86 pp with the annotated target end.
In Figure S1 a long run of identical digital samples complicates interpretation.
text.formatted: In Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref> a long run of identical digital samples complicates interpretation.

text.text: Figure S2 shows a second V3 excursion outside the automatic window without a repeated 12-lead sample in that QRS.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S2</ref> shows a second V3 excursion outside the automatic window without a repeated 12-lead sample in that QRS.

text.text: Both observations concern the recorded waveform.
Neither establishes the physiological origin of the deflection.
V3 had the largest estimated change in relative model benefit (Holm-adjusted p = 0.060).
Across test patients, mean RMSE fell from 10.64 to 3.33 pp when both coefficients could be fitted afresh to each measured target window (a reduction of 68.74%).
The fit had access to the same 20 samples used to score it and could absorb noise as well as signal.
Baseline uncertainty and similar V1 and V6 waveforms can both affect the residual.
Its magnitude alone cannot identify an unmeasured electrical source.
This was an internal test in a single database already used by the investigators.
Development and test patients were separate, but acquisition and annotation practices were shared.
The normalization preserves relative amplitude within a channel and removes between-lead and between-patient differences in peak-to-peak amplitude.
Recovering a missing target in clinical units would require its scale, which cannot be obtained from these data.
Filtering in both directions and centred moving averages used later samples.
Normalization and detector thresholds used the full ten-second record.
The paired timing comparison further required a suitable automatic anchor and disproportionately lost beats from recordings labelled with ventricular pacing.
Each lead has one published set of boundaries, precluding an estimate of inter-reader variability.
The six annotations identify a common QRS by the stated rule.
They do not establish an exact physiological end.
Actual electrode loss, patient-level diagnostic decisions and effects on management were not studied.
One preset angle per lead was sufficient to improve the offline estimate of relative amplitude in the last 40 ms of V3, V4 and V5 in held-out LUDB patients.
The largest gains were in V3 and V4, where the V1/V6 projection reduced mean error by about one fifth compared with the fitted single lead.
The result for V2 remained uncertain.
This gives a reduced-lead recording a way to estimate the terminal waveform of an unavailable precordial lead without fitting the projection to that patient.
The voltage of an individual deflection and the diagnostic accuracy of a reconstructed notch or slur still require validation against directly measured leads.
Terminal window: the 20 samples scored at the end of a target QRS.
Fixed projection: the weighted sum of V1 and V6 at each sample, using one population angle for each target.
Exclusive stop: the first sample outside the scoring window.
RMSE: the square root of the mean squared normalized amplitude difference within one window.

The supplementary archive contains the Python programs, fixed model coefficients, record assignments and individual measurements.
Its README.md explains how to reproduce the numerical results, figures and supplementary appendix from the public release.
Figure 1: Time-embedded ECG and its fixed V3 projection.
Panel A shows the rangenormalized V1 and V6 signals throughout the annotated QRS of LUDB record 28 (V3 peak at sample 2236).
The open circle marks the annotated V3 onset.
The curve runs out and returns as time advances upwards.
The orange segment contains the final 20 samples, ending at the diamond.
Panel B shows the projection and the simultaneously measured V3.
The shaded interval contains samples from -40 to -2 ms.
Zero is the first sample after the annotated closing sample.
This beat was nearest the median V3 test error.
V3 peak 4060 • High correlation (r = 0.973) • RMSE 14.73 pp
Figure2: Measured and reconstructed V3 complexes.
The first two panels were selected by proximity to the median and 99th percentile of V3 projection error.
The third panel shows record 78, V3 peak 4060 (correlation 0.973, terminal RMSE 14.73 pp).
Among V3 complexes with whole-QRS correlation of at least 0.95 and terminal RMSE of at least 10 pp, its error was tied for closest to the median.
The lower record identifier determined the selection.
Amplitudes are percentages of each channel's 10-second range.
Shading marks the 40 ms ending at the annotated V3 boundary.
Time zero is the exclusive annotated stop.
The dashed line marks the exclusive automatic stop and coincides with the annotated stop in the third panel.
The single-lead fit had lower error than the projection in the first two examples.
Terminal RMSE and paired differences in 80 test participants.
Errors and differences are in pp.
The global p value is unadjusted.
Lead-specific p values are Holmadjusted.
A positive difference favours the projection.
Effect of changing the end of the QRS in the same 702 beats.
Each pair of entries gives the automatic value first and the annotated value second.
Change is the annotated minus automatic advantage.
Values and patient-bootstrap 95% intervals are in pp.
